paper_title: PrismaCoder: Pushing the Boundaries of Open Multimodal Code Intelligence through Decomposed Rubric Synthesis

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Multimodal code intelligence connects the symbolic world of programs with the visual world their execution creates. Interest in this capability is burgeoning, as models are increasingly asked to produce charts, webpages, animations, and semi-structured documents. Recently, proprietary models have pushed far ahead, producing interactive artifacts even from a text description or a screenshot alone. Yet their data and training remain closed, and open progress is held back by the quantity and quality of available data and by the pipelines and methods for producing it. Quality is the harder of the two, since a sample must be correct as a program, well built, and above all visually right once rendered. No existing signal covers all three. Execution often returns just a pass or fail, code similarity does not map to the visual output, and task-specific verifiers do not generalize. To push open progress further, we start from the data side with PrismaForge, a hierarchical data pipeline centered on a synthesized rubric that decomposes these factors into checkable criteria. The same rubric serves as both filter and reward: it curates the supervised corpus, then drives reinforcement learning on visual-coding tasks. Leveraging PrismaForge for data synthesis and filtering, we build PrismaCoder-2M, the most diverse open dataset for multimodal code intelligence and the largest to date. On the model side, we train PrismaCoder-9B and PrismaCoder-35B on this data and release both. They lead the open state of the art by a wide margin and rival leading proprietary systems. Our analyses further show that the proposed rubric-based pipeline improves multimodal coding performance across model backbones. We release our code and data at https://qiushisun.github.io/PrismaCoder-Home/.

Our analyses further show that the proposed rubric-based pipeline improves multimodal coding performance across model backbones. We release our code, model, and data at the PrismaCoder Homepage. 1. Introduction From symbols to pixels, code intelligence now extends beyond textual source code into the visual world that programs produce (Zan et al., 2023; Sun et al., 2024; Zhao et al., 2026). growing range of applications specifies intent through images and judges result by what its code renders, from charts and web pages to diagrams, typeset documents, and animations. Leading proprietary systems now produce interactive artifacts from text description or screenshot alone. Prior open efforts have mostly addressed one corner of this space at time, from plotting (Ni et al., 2025b; Galimzyanov et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2024) and chart-to-code (Yang et al., 2025a; Zhao et al., 2025c) to screenshot-to-page generation (Gui et al., 2025; Si et al., 2025). Each comes with its own data and recipe, making it difficult for the resulting models to generalize across task domains and output formats. Recently, open work such as JanusCoder (Sun et al., 2026b) has brought many of these scenarios under shared visual-programmatic interface, with follow-up refinements building on the same view (Zhao et al., 2025a; Jiang et al., 2026; Ni et al., 2026). Despite these advances, publicly available training data remains limited in scale and uneven in quality, with only handful of open releases and resources to Contact author(s): qiushisun@connect.hku.hk, jingyang.gong@connect.hku.hk, ggaojiahui@gmail.com * Equal contribution # Corresponding author PrismaCoder: Open Multimodal Code Intelligence through Decomposed Rubric Synthesis Figure 1: Scenarios and formats covered by PrismaCoder-2M and PrismaCoder. date (Sun et al., 2026b; Jiang et al., 2026). The pipelines used to build these datasets are rarely released, while proprietary systems keep their data and training closed. Moreover, existing public data are typically curated with either single per-sample score, which provides limited diagnostic information about errors, or task-specific verifier, which does not generalize across tasks. To address this gap, we introduce PrismaForge, rubric-based framework for multimodal code data curation and policy optimization. Rather than relying solely on holistic judgment or fixed checklist, PrismaForge applies common evaluation procedure across data sources and task domains while tailoring its criteria to each instruction. Each rubric combines reusable domain-level checks with instruction-specific requirements, with the number of criteria adjusted to the estimated task difficulty. Code-level and visual-level criteria are evaluated separately on the generated program and its rendered artifact, respectively. These scores guide data curation and serve as reinforcement learning rewards. Using PrismaForge, we curate PrismaCoder-2M, the broadest open dataset to date for advancing multimodal code intelligence, spanning more than 12 categories and 10 programming languages with both text-centric and vision-centric data. To build this coverage, we draw seeds from complementary sources: public visual-coding corpora cover common plotting and graphics tasks; research figures and open-source repositories contribute long-tail scientific examples; and web, interactive-demo, and chemicalstructure sources broaden the range of artifacts. We then convert the seeds into self-contained tasks, check candidate programs through format-specific execution and rendering, and use instruction-specific rubric scores to filter or refine the resulting examples. This gives the dataset both breadth of coverage and consistent quality-control process. To assess whether the breadth of PrismaCoder-2M translates into broad model capability, we develop PrismaCoder-9B and PrismaCoder-35B. Evaluated on wide range of representative benchmarks, PrismaCoder leads the existing open state of the art by wide margin and matches the proprietary systems to considerable degree (5). Through extensive analyses (6), we show that the data and pipeline generalize across base models beyond our release. We further show that rubric-guided curation outperforms direct-judge selection and that rubric scores align closely with human judgments. Our main contributions are summarized as follows: Decomposed Rubric Synthesis for Visual-coding Data. We introduce PrismaForge, principled pipeline whose hierarchically synthesized rubrics serve as both filter and reward. Based on it, we 2 PrismaCoder: Open Multimodal Code Intelligence through Decomposed Rubric Synthesis curate PrismaCoder-2M, the broadest and largest open dataset to date. Open Models that Rival Proprietary Systems. We build PrismaCoder-9B/35B on PrismaCoder2M, which lead the open state of the art by wide margin and match or surpass leading proprietary systems on charts, front-end pages, and semi-structured documents. Empirical Insights across Data, Modeling, and Training. Beyond data and model contributions, we further share insights through extensive analysis. It shows that our pipeline generalizes across scenarios and backbones and yields artifacts better aligned with human preference. 2. Related Work Multimodal Code Intelligence. Code intelligence now extends beyond text-only programming to visual-programmatic tasks, where intent may be visual (Li et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024a; Wang et al., 2025) and outputs can be judged only after execution or rendering (Zhao et al., 2026). On the output side, syntactic validity is insufficient; correctness also depends on layout, semantics, interaction, and editability. On the input side, reading values and layout off renders remains perception bottleneck (Masry et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2024; Xia et al., 2025) across vision-language models (Zhang et al., 2024b; Liu et al., 2025). The tasks run from screenshot-to-code (Gui et al., 2025; Si et al., 2025; Yun et al., 2024) to front-end engineering (Jiang et al., 2025; Zhu et al., 2025; Sun et al., 2025a) and generative UI (Zheng et al., 2026); chart generation (Yang et al., 2025a; Zhao et al., 2025c; Wu et al., 2025) and editing (Zhang et al., 2024c; Zhao et al., 2025b); SVG and symbolic graphics (Yang et al., 2025b; Nishina & Matsui, 2024; Xu et al., 2024) with their structural probes (Qiu et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025b); and interactive artifacts and code-driven demonstrations (Zhang et al., 2025; Ku et al., 2025; Sun et al., 2025b). Recent generalists unify these domains via JanusCoders visual-programmatic interface (Sun et al., 2026b), VisCodexs visioncode integration (Jiang et al., 2026), VisCoder2s agentic visualization coding (Ni et al., 2026), and VinciCoders visual reinforcement learning (Zhao et al., 2025a). Yet shared modeling interface does not by itself make heterogeneous notions of correctness consistently measurable or usable for training (Zhao et al., 2026). Complementing this progress, we contribute on the data side, with PrismaCoder-2M spanning the broadest scenarios and open data types. Learning Signals for Code Generation. Conventional code tasks (Zhang et al., 2023) draw training data from instruction synthesis and evolution (Wei et al., 2024; Luo et al., 2024, 2025b). For many such tasks, executable tests provide cheap, reproducible signal for data filtering (Xu et al., 2025b; Sun et al., 2026a) and reinforcement learning (Shao et al., 2024; Xu et al., 2025a; Zhuo et al., 2025). Visual outputs break this assumption: successful execution confirms only that the code runs, not that its render is faithful, well composed, or semantically correct (Zhao et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026; Guo et al., 2025). Visual benchmarks instead use task-specific render checks for charts (Yang et al., 2025a), visual and structural similarity for web pages (Si et al., 2025), or judge protocols for interactive artifacts (Zhang et al., 2025); effective individually, these measures do not compose across artifacts. Recent work moves toward finer supervision, from JanusCoders single-pass rubric over fixed dimensions (Sun et al., 2026b) to VinciCoders coarse-to-fine rewards (Zhao et al., 2025a). Neither signal is yet both fine enough to localize failures and general enough to cover every task, at curation and at training alike. In this work, one synthesized rubric per instruction serves both roles, filtering the training data and rewarding reinforcement learning across every format we cover. 3 PrismaCoder: Open Multimodal Code Intelligence through Decomposed Rubric Synthesis Figure 2: PrismaForge writes one rubric per instruction and uses it twice, to filter candidate data into PrismaCoder-2M and to reward rollouts in reinforcement learning. 3. PrismaForge In this section, we present PrismaForge, rubric-based scoring framework that lies in the center of our data curation and training pipeline. 3.1. Elastic Rubric Scorer For large-scale coding dataset prepared for visualization or demonstration, the key challenge is to determine which candidates are sufficiently correct and useful to retain. Unlike problems with easily verifiable outputs, visualization quality is often specified only implicitly (Wu et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2025a). single holistic score is therefore hard to verify and offers little insight into why candidate succeeds or fails (Ye et al., 2024; Sun et al., 2026b). natural alternative is to evaluate candidates using explicit criteria, but fixed rubric is too coarse for diverse visualization tasks. Different instructions may prioritize numerical accuracy and axis scales, visual similarity, layout, or artifact editability. universal rubric must stay broad and may miss the properties most important for specific example. At the other extreme, manually designing separate rubrics for every visualization instruction would require substantial human effort and is hard to scale. We release PrismaCoder-9B and PrismaCoder-35B-A3B (abbreviated as PrismaCoder35B), post-trained from Qwen3.5-9B and Qwen3.5-35B-A3B (Qwen Team, 2026). We also train Gemma4-31B-it (Gemma Team, 2026) and Qwen3-VL-30B-A3B-Instruct (Bai et al., 2025). More training details are in Appendix F. Data Pipeline Details. We reprocess data from prior open releases (Sun et al., 2026b; Jiang et al., 2026; Ni et al., 2026). PrismaForge treats its models as pluggable, and in this paper we use Claude-Opus-4.6 (Anthropic, 2026a) as the curation model and Gemini-3-Pro (Gemini Team, 2025) as the rubric generator. Both data gating and reinforcement learning use Gemini 3 Flash as the judge. The sources are listed per category in Appendix B. Baselines. Besides Qwen3.5, we compare against open multimodal code models, namely JanusCoderV (Sun et al., 2026b), VinciCoder (Zhao et al., 2025a), and VisCoder2-7B (Ni et al., 2026). 8 PrismaCoder: Open Multimodal Code Intelligence through Decomposed Rubric Synthesis 5.2. Benchmarking Vision-Centric Settings. The vision-centric suite comprises ChartMimic (Yang et al., 2025a), WebCode2M (Gui et al., 2025), DesignBench (Xiao et al., 2025), Design2Code (Si et al., 2025), and ChemDraw (Zhao et al., 2025a), together with the image-conditioned lenses of InteractScience (Chen et al., 2025a) (VQT) and UniSVG (Li et al., 2025) (ISVGen). Text-Centric Settings. The text-centric suite comprises ArtifactsBench (Zhang et al., 2025), PandasPlotBench (Galimzyanov et al., 2025), and VisPlotBench (Ni et al., 2026) in eight visualization languages, together with InteractSciences programmatic lens (PFT) and UniSVGs text-conditioned lens (TSVGen). Evaluation Protocol. Evaluation follows each benchmarks official protocol, with deterministic metrics reported alongside judge scores. Since some designated judges share model family with our pipeline, we check that the gains hold across judges (6.3). Details are presented in E. 5.3. Vision-Centric Results Web Interfaces. Rubric Efficacy To intuitively demonstrate the advantages of the rubric-based method over direct judging, we fine-tune Qwen3.5-9B on two equal-sized subsets drawn from the same data pool. One is filtered by direct scoring, where judge assigns each sample single holistic score as in typical pipeline (Sun et al., 2026b), and the other by the PrismaForge rubric. The model trained on the 10 PrismaCoder: Open Multimodal Code Intelligence through Decomposed Rubric Synthesis Figure 5: PrismaForge filtering outperforms direct-judge filtering on every benchmark. Figure 6: Per-stage gains of our SFT and RL pipeline over two base models on every metric. rubric-filtered subset scores higher on every benchmark, by as much as 24 points on Vega-Lite  (Fig. 5)  . The gains are largest on the text-centric formats and small on the vision-centric benchmarks, where Design2Code moves by fraction of point. Since both subsets have the same size, the gap reflects which samples each judge keeps. 6.2. Backbone Generalization Beyond the released Qwen3.5 backbones, we apply the same data and method to Gemma-4-31Bit (Gemma Team, 2026) and Qwen3-VL-30B-A3B-Instruct (Bai et al., 2025) on Python plotting and HTML, the two most represented domains. On both backbones all twelve metrics end above the base model, and RL adds to SFT on every one  (Fig. 6)  . SFT carries most of the ChartMimic gain, whereas RL drives most of the HTML gains and recovers every metric that dips after SFT alone. More results on Gemma are presented in Appendix H.1. 11 PrismaCoder: Open Multimodal Code Intelligence through Decomposed Rubric Synthesis 6.3. Rubric Agreement with Humans Because multimodal code artifacts are ultimately created for humans, consistency with human judgment provides compelling test to verify that the quality of data yielded by our rubric-based PrismaForge aligns more closely with human preferences. At the same time, preserving the relative ordering induced by scores is particularly important for reward-based policy optimization, where inconsistent rankings can provide conflicting training signals. To evaluate our method along both dimensions, we conducted human study. We sampled 100 examples from our training data and asked human annotators, as well as three proprietary model judges, to evaluate them using direct scoring and the PrismaForge rubrics, respectively. We then measured the agreement between each model judge and the human ratings in terms of both absolute score levels and pairwise ordering  (Fig. 7)  . The rubric-based judging method achieves substantially higher agreement with human judgments and greater consistency in the induced partial ordering across all three model judges. The full study protocol and detailed statistics are provided in Appendix H.2. We further show that the gains of our pipeline hold across judge models, with the experiments presented in Appendix H.1. Figure 7: PrismaForge scoring aligns judges with humans better than direct scoring. 7. Conclusion In this work, we push open multimodal code intelligence forward by jointly contributing and fully releasing data, pipeline, and models. PrismaForge treats multimodal code data under one lens with rubrics synthesized from coarse to fine and decomposed into code-level and visual-level criteria, signal that both generalizes and localizes what went wrong. We then curate and release PrismaCoder-2M, the most broadly covering open dataset for multimodal code intelligence, which enables principled selection and stable reinforcement learning on visual-coding tasks. On this data we build PrismaCoder-9B/35B, which lead the open state of the art by wide margin and rival proprietary systems. Extensive analyses across base models and task recipes show that the data and the pipeline generalize beyond our release, and we share these insights and resources to broaden access to visual-coding capabilities.

sections.content: 33 A. Data Toolkit Details A.1. AST-Based Decomposition Plotting scripts collected from GitHub and Manim scene files are often long, and one file may draw several figures. For such data, we parse each script into an abstract syntax tree without executing it and split it into self-contained units. unit is the code that produces one figure in plotting script, or one scene in Manim file (a class inheriting from Scene). Each unit keeps the imports and statements it depends on, drops project-private helpers that exist only in the source repository, and carries its embedded text and short excerpt as features. The units are stored as structured entries that the synthesis pipeline and the gatekeeper of Section 4.2 read. Rubric Synthesis Prompts and Examples Web UI reconstruction must be evaluated from two complementary perspectives: whether the generated HTML/CSS implements the required content and structure, and whether its rendered output reproduces the intended visual appearance. single holistic score often conflates these two aspects and provides little evidence about the source of an error. We therefore synthesize two sets of sample-specific binary rubrics from the task instruction and reference screenshot. Code rubrics target properties that can be verified directly from the implementation, whereas vision rubrics target properties observable in the rendered page. Figs. 8 and 9 show the corresponding prompt templates. Both prompts organize checks into shared quality criteria and sample-dependent requirements, and assign each check weight according to its importance. The difficulty level assigned to the instruction enters both prompts as an item budget, so harder samples receive more criteria (3.1). The templates are abridged to remove repetitive wording. The complementary roles of the two rubric views are illustrated by the representative reconstruction in Fig. 3. Code rubrics verify that the expected elements and implementation constraints are present, whereas vision rubrics reveal rendering failures that may remain hidden in otherwise valid HTML/CSS. In this example, the synthesized page preserves the references overall content, colors, and organization, yet contains salient local layout failure. It receives perfect code-rubric score of 1.0, indicating that the implementation contains the expected structure and content. It also obtains holistic LLM judgment score of 78, outperforming approximately 78.6% of all samples. Nevertheless, our sample-specific vision rubrics assign an aggregate score of only 0.182. They identify that the footer is incorrectly positioned in the middle of the page, where it overlaps and clips the third service button and disrupts the intended vertical hierarchy. They also capture that the synthesized buttons have square rather than rounded corners. We next examine the individual judgments that produce this discrepancy. However, there is layout error where the footer is positioned too high, overlapping the Service 3 button and leaving empty space at the bottom. Thus, the holistic evaluator notices the dominant layout error but compresses it into relatively high scalar score. The rubric-based evaluation both amplifies its impact according to sample-specific requirements and identifies the additional corner-shape and content-visibility failures. These localized but perceptually important errors are easily diluted in single holistic similarity score, whereas our fine-grained rubrics explicitly expose and penalize each failure. The two rubric views thus provide more diagnostic and structurally sensitive feedback than code inspection or holistic visual judgment alone. In our experiments, we use Gemini-3-Flash for rubrics. For common visualization tasks, such as Python plotting, the average cost of generating rubrics for single sample is approximately $0.006 based on the official API pricing, while evaluating the generated code and visual artifacts costs approximately $0.01 per sample. For HTML-related tasks, the input cost is substantially higher because rich, complex websites typically involve much longer HTML code. In these cases, rubric generation costs approximately $0.01 per sample, while evaluation costs approximately $0.04. D. RL Reward Specification This appendix specifies the reward computation procedure behind 3.2. For each rollout response 𝑐(𝑘) , the procedure first extracts code from the response text. For Python, we extract the longest fenced code block. For HTML, we extract single complete document spanning from the doctype declaration to the closing tag. For SVG, we extract either the code contained in fenced block or the first complete <svg> span. completion that does not contain valid code of the required type is assigned reward of 0 without further evaluation. 𝑖 dispatcher then routes each rollout to exactly one task family, and the scorer registered for that family returns reward in [0, 1], where 1 denotes fully satisfactory solution. An unscoreable completion (due to missing or malformed answer, unavailable rubric or reference material, execution or rendering failure, or judge failure that persists after retries) receives reward of 0. The basic reward computation for each task largely follows Eq. 2 and Eq. 3. Specifically, the response code and the rendered visual artifact are scored separately and then aggregated using weighted average. We use different combinations of code-score and visual-score weights across task families. This is because for tasks such as Python plotting, correct data representation and placement are as important as visual integrity and presentation quality. In contrast, for educational demonstration artifacts, visual readiness and interactivity are often more important than the particular implementation used to produce them. We found, however, that predefined rubrics alone may fail to capture certain forms of misalignment in few tasks such as interface reproduction. Instructions for these tasks inherently allow some flexibility in content generation, particularly with respect to styling and layout organization. As result, some errors or mismatches can only be assessed reliably after the generated page is viewed alongside the reference page. To address this limitation, we introduce complementary holistic score for task families of this type. This score is combined with the rubric-based scores using weight denoted by 𝜆ℎ. In this way, the evaluation retains the consistency and structure of rubric-based scoring while also capturing qualitative discrepancies that become apparent only when the generated artifact is evaluated as whole. 23 PrismaCoder: Open Multimodal Code Intelligence through Decomposed Rubric Synthesis The reward logic and the weight combinations used for each task domain are summarized in Tab. 7. Benchmark Details and Evaluation Settings Code-driven video and animation, and theorem and symbolic visualization, are released as training data only and are not part of the evaluation. Vision-Centric Benchmarks. ChartMimic reproduces chart from its image; its Direct split regenerates the chart and its Customized split edits an existing one, scored by low-level element extraction (text, layout, type, color) and high-level judge score. WebCode2M, DesignBench, and Design2Code cover front-end generation from screenshot: WebCode2M buckets pages by length and reports judge score, visual similarity, CLIP, and TreeBLEU; DesignBench scores generation and editing with judge score plus CLIP, MAE, SSIM, and CMS; Design2Code reports element-level block, text, position, and color matches, CLIP, and judge score. InteractSciences visual lens (VQT) is visually grounded qualitative test judged by visionlanguage model. UniSVGs image-conditioned lens (ISVGen) reproduces an image as SVG. ChemDraw measures execution rate, molecule validity, exact match, and Tanimoto similarity. Text-Centric Benchmarks. ArtifactsBench reports an overall score over ten artifact domains. PandasPlotBench reports the incorrect-code rate and mean and Good(75) scores under visual and task lens. InteractSciences programmatic lens (PFT) is functional test over the generated demonstration. UniSVGs text-conditioned lens (TSVGen) generates SVG from text. VisPlotBench covers eight languages with the same metrics as PandasPlotBench, using its designated judge GPT-4.1 (OpenAI, 2025). Evaluation Settings. Evaluation follows the benchmarks official protocol, including its designated judge model where one is specified, so that our numbers stay comparable with published results. Due to the availability of legacy models, ChartMimics high-level score is judged by GPT-5.5 (OpenAI, 2026) instead of the original GPT-4o. 24 PrismaCoder: Open Multimodal Code Intelligence through Decomposed Rubric Synthesis F. Training Details All experiments were conducted on four interconnected compute nodes, each equipped with 8 NVIDIA H200 GPUs, for total of 32 GPUs. We used the Megatron backend in the ms-swift framework for distributed SFT and RL. Both stages performed full-parameter fine-tuning with FlashAttention and sequence parallelism enabled. Activation recomputation reduced memory use throughout training. For SFT, we initialized from Qwen3.5-9B/Qwen3.5-35B-A3B and trained the language model for 5 epochs. We used maximum sequence length of 32,768 tokens and enabled sequence packing for improved token utilization. The global batch size was set to be 128. The learning rate peaked at 1 105, with warm-up fraction of 5%, and decayed to minimum learning rate of 5 107. For RL, we initialized from the SFT checkpoint and performed one epoch of GRPO/GSPO. We implemented rubric-based reward plugin following the methodology described in Section 3.2 and Appendix D. For the judge model 𝐿𝐽 used to evaluate online rollouts, we selected Gemini-3-Flash to balance evaluation quality and cost. The global training batch size was 512 in terms of rollouts (equivalent to 64 samples per batch) and 8 candidate responses were generated per prompt at each rollout step. Rollout generation was performed with colocated vLLM inference using tensor parallelism of size 8 and maximum model length of 36,000 tokens. Sampling used temperature of 1.0 and top-𝑝 of 0.95. The GRPO/GSPO learning rate was set to 3 106. We used KL regularization coefficient of 𝛽 = 0.04, and asymmetric clipping thresholds of 𝜖 = 0.20 and 𝜖high = 0.28. Dynamic sampling and overlongresponse filtering were enabled during rollout collection. Training was conducted in BF16 precision, with model and optimizer offloading enabled to reduce GPU memory usage. G. Full Per-Benchmark Results Each benchmark reports several metrics; the main text shows compact headline set per benchmark, and the complete metric sets are here, one table per benchmark, mirroring our evaluation workbook. G.1. Visualization ChartMimic. The complete results of the direct-1800 split of the ChartMimic benchmark is shown in Table 8. We can see that PrismaCoder shows strong performance against both open and proprietary models. PrismaCoder-9B achieves an overall score of 77.70, substantially outperforming other similarly sized open models (around 7273) and even surpassing GPT-4o (74.20). Scaling to PrismaCoder-35B further improves the overall score to 82.05, with particularly strong execution rate (96.16), text fidelity (90.41), layout (94.00), and GPT-based similarity (80.69). WebDev WebCode2M. Table 14 shows that PrismaCoders advantage is consistent across webpages of different code lengths. PrismaCoder-9B obtains Visual scores of 90.06, 90.02, and 91.15 on the short, mid, and long subsets, respectively, while its LLM score remains similarly stable across the three groups. CLIP similarity decreases modestly with page length, from 90.29 to 87.32, but remains well above the prior open models throughout. The main exception is TreeBLEU: both PrismaCoder models score below JanusCoder and VinciCoder despite producing substantially more faithful renderings according to the visual metrics. This difference arises because TreeBLEU measures similarity to the reference HTML tree rather than the rendered webpage itself. JanusCoder and VinciCoder are trained on the original WebCode2M code, which naturally favors reproducing structures similar to the benchmark references. PrismaCoder instead uses regenerated code paired with webpages rendered from that code, rather than directly using the original WebCode2M source code. This regeneration is intentional. The original WebCode2M code comes from diverse real-world webpages and can differ substantially from the code distribution naturally produced by LLMs. Using regenerated code therefore better aligns the training targets with inference-time generations, while re-rendering the regenerated programs ensures exact consistency between the code and its visual target. Its generated webpages can consequently closely match the target appearance without following the particular HTML or DOM structure of the reference implementation. The similarly low TreeBLEU scores of the proprietary models further illustrate that reference-code similarity does not necessarily track rendering fidelity. DesignBench.
